Full name: Aiding and abetting; principal liability
What it covers: Whoever aids, abets, counsels, commands, induces, or procures a federal offense is punishable as a principal. Requires intent to facilitate the offense and knowledge of its essential facts.

Full name: Conspiracy to commit offense or defraud the United States
What it covers: Agreement of two or more persons to commit a federal offense or defraud the United States, plus an overt act.

Full name: Wire fraud
What it covers: Scheme to defraud or obtain money or property by false pretenses using interstate wire, radio, or internet communications.

Full name: Bank fraud
What it covers: Scheme to defraud a financial institution or obtain its funds by false pretenses (e.g., voice-cloned authorization of transfers).

Full name: Identity fraud; aggravated identity theft
What it covers: Knowingly transferring, possessing, or using another person's means of identification in connection with unlawful activity; mandatory consecutive term when used during enumerated felonies such as wire fraud.

Full name: Computer Fraud and Abuse Act
What it covers: Accessing a computer without authorization or exceeding authorized access; knowingly transmitting code that intentionally causes damage; computer-based extortion; trafficking in passwords.

Full name: Interstate threats and extortion (incl. sextortion)
What it covers: Transmitting in interstate commerce a threat to injure a person, or a threat to injure reputation or accuse of a crime with intent to extort money or a thing of value.
Mental state required: intent to extort; for true threats at least recklessness (Counterman v. Colorado)

Full name: Cyberstalking
What it covers: Using electronic communication services in a course of conduct, with intent to kill, injure, harass, intimidate, or place under surveillance, that places a person in reasonable fear or causes substantial emotional distress.

Full name: Obscene or harassing telecommunications
What it covers: Making or initiating communications that are obscene or child pornography with intent to abuse, threaten, or harass; repeated harassing calls or communications.

Full name: TAKE IT DOWN Act: publishing nonconsensual intimate images and digital forgeries
What it covers: Using an interactive computer service to knowingly publish an intimate visual depiction, or an AI-made digital forgery indistinguishable from an authentic one, of an identifiable person without consent, where publication is intended to or does cause harm (adults: up to 2 years); publishing a forgery of a minor to abuse, humiliate, harass, degrade, or sexually gratify (up to 3 years); threats to publish; mandatory forfeiture and restitution.
Mental state required: knowledge; intent to harm or actual harm

Full name: Child sexual abuse material (incl. morphed images of identifiable minors)
What it covers: Knowingly producing, distributing, receiving, or possessing child pornography, defined to include computer-generated images indistinguishable from a minor and images modified to appear to depict an identifiable minor.

Full name: Obscene visual representations of the sexual abuse of children
What it covers: Knowingly producing, distributing, receiving, or possessing obscene visual depictions of any kind (drawing, cartoon, computer-generated image) of a minor engaged in sexually explicit conduct; the statute says the depicted minor need not actually exist.

Full name: Transfer of obscene material to a minor
What it covers: Knowingly transferring obscene matter through the mail or interstate means to a person under 16, knowing the person is under 16, or attempting to; up to 10 years.

Full name: Coercion and enticement of a minor
What it covers: Using interstate facilities to knowingly persuade, induce, entice, or coerce a minor to engage in sexual activity for which any person could be charged.

Full name: Distributing information on explosives, destructive devices, or WMD
What it covers: Teaching or demonstrating the making or use of an explosive, destructive device, or weapon of mass destruction, or distributing information about it, either intending that it be used for a federal crime of violence, or knowing that the recipient intends to use it for one.
Mental state required: intent or knowledge of intended violent use

Full name: Biological, chemical, and mass-destruction weapons
What it covers: Developing, producing, acquiring, or knowingly assisting a foreign state or organization with biological or chemical weapons; using or attempting/conspiring to use a weapon of mass destruction.

Full name: Material support to terrorists
What it covers: Providing material support or resources, including expert advice or assistance, knowing or intending they will be used to prepare or carry out enumerated terrorism offenses.

Full name: Solicitation to commit a crime of violence
What it covers: With intent that another person engage in a federal crime of violence, soliciting, commanding, inducing, or otherwise endeavoring to persuade that person to do so, under circumstances strongly corroborative of that intent.

Full name: Securities fraud and market manipulation
What it covers: Willful use of manipulative or deceptive devices, material misstatements, or schemes to defraud in connection with buying or selling securities, including pump-and-dump schemes driven by fake news.

Full name: Commodities spoofing and manipulation
What it covers: Bidding or offering with intent to cancel before execution (spoofing), and manipulation of commodity or futures prices.
Mental state required: intent; knowing violation for criminal penalty

Full name: Sherman Act section 1 (price fixing, collusion)
What it covers: Contracts, combinations, or conspiracies in restraint of trade, including competitors fixing prices through a shared pricing algorithm or intermediary; per se illegal price fixing is a felony.

Full name: Health care fraud; false statements in health care matters
What it covers: Knowingly executing a scheme to defraud a health care benefit program, or making false statements in connection with delivery of or payment for health care benefits.

Full name: Wiretap Act interception
What it covers: Intentionally intercepting, disclosing, or using the contents of wire, oral, or electronic communications without a party's consent (one-party consent federal rule).

Full name: Wrongful disclosure of individually identifiable health information
What it covers: Knowingly obtaining or disclosing individually identifiable health information in violation of HIPAA's administrative simplification rules; heavier penalties for false pretenses or commercial advantage.

Full name: Theft of trade secrets
What it covers: Knowingly stealing, copying, or receiving a trade secret intending to convert it to the economic benefit of someone other than the owner.

Full name: Criminal copyright infringement
What it covers: Willful copyright infringement for commercial advantage or private financial gain, or above value thresholds.

Full name: Deprivation of rights under color of law
What it covers: Willfully depriving a person of constitutional or federal rights while acting under color of law (e.g., an officer making an arrest knowing it lacks probable cause).

Full name: Conspiracy against rights (incl. the right to vote)
What it covers: Two or more persons conspiring to injure, oppress, threaten, or intimidate a person in the free exercise of a federal right, including voting. Its use against voting disinformation is unsettled: the Second Circuit reversed the Mackey text-to-vote meme conviction in 2025 for lack of proof of an agreement, without deciding whether § 241 reaches that conduct (United States v. Mackey, 143 F.4th 129 (2d Cir. 2025)).

Full name: Voter intimidation; election fraud
What it covers: Intimidating, threatening, or coercing any person to interfere with the right to vote in a federal election; knowingly and willfully defrauding residents of a fair election process.

Full name: Impersonating a federal officer or employee
What it covers: Falsely assuming or pretending to be a federal officer or employee and acting as such, or demanding or obtaining anything of value in that pretended character.

Full name: False statements to the federal government
What it covers: Knowingly and willfully making a materially false statement or using a false document in a matter within federal jurisdiction (e.g., fabricated material submitted to a federal agency).

Full name: False declarations before a court
What it covers: Knowingly making a false material declaration, or using a document knowing it contains a false material declaration, in a federal court or grand jury proceeding.

Full name: False information and hoaxes; swatting
What it covers: Conveying false or misleading information under circumstances where it may reasonably be believed, indicating that an act of violence or terrorism is taking place or will take place.

Full name: FDCA prohibited acts (misbranded or adulterated devices and drugs)
What it covers: Introducing misbranded or adulterated medical devices or drugs (including unapproved software functions that are devices) into interstate commerce. First offense is a strict-liability misdemeanor reaching responsible corporate officers under United States v. Park.
Mental state required: none for misdemeanor; intent to defraud for felony

Full name: Willful OSHA violation causing death
What it covers: An employer who willfully violates an OSHA standard or rule, where the violation causes an employee's death (e.g., unguarded industrial robots).

Full name: False or misleading vehicle safety reports
What it covers: Violating 18 U.S.C. § 1001 in reports required by 49 U.S.C. § 30166, with the specific intent to mislead NHTSA about safety defects that caused death or serious bodily injury; up to 15 years. A correction safe harbor applies (49 C.F.R. § 578.7, NHTSA final rule 2001).

Full name: Controlled substance distribution and use of communication facility
What it covers: Knowingly distributing or dispensing controlled substances without authorization; using a phone or the internet to facilitate a drug felony.

Full name: Accessory liability as a principal (state)
What it covers: Anyone who commits, or aids, abets, counsels, hires, or otherwise procures, a criminal offense that is committed or attempted is a principal in the first degree and may be charged, convicted, and punished as such, present or not (Fla.); California treats aiders and abettors as principals. Florida's Attorney General invoked this theory against ChatGPT over the FSU shooting in April 2026.
Mental state required: intent that the crime be committed (Florida); knowledge and intent (California)

Full name: Murder, manslaughter, criminally negligent homicide
What it covers: Unlawful killing with malice (murder) or without malice through a lawful act done without due caution or through culpable negligence (involuntary manslaughter).

Full name: Vehicular manslaughter / negligent homicide by vehicle
Citation: Cal. Penal Code § 192(c); Ariz. Rev. Stat. § 13-1102
What it covers: Killing a person while driving with ordinary or gross negligence (California), or causing death with criminal negligence (Arizona; the statute used against the safety driver in the 2018 Uber Tempe crash).
Mental state required: ordinary or gross negligence / criminal negligence

Full name: Assault and battery
What it covers: Unlawful attempt to commit a violent injury (assault) or willful and unlawful use of force or violence on another person (battery).

Full name: Reckless endangerment
What it covers: Recklessly engaging in conduct that creates a substantial risk of serious physical injury (second degree) or, with depraved indifference, a grave risk of death (first degree).

Full name: Aiding, advising, or encouraging suicide; manslaughter by encouragement
Citation: Cal. Penal Code § 401; Commonwealth v. Carter, 481 Mass. 352 (2019)
What it covers: Deliberately aiding, advising, or encouraging another to die by suicide (felony in California); in Massachusetts, wanton or reckless pressure on a person to complete a suicide supported an involuntary manslaughter conviction.

Full name: Child endangerment
What it covers: Willfully causing or permitting a child to suffer unjustifiable physical pain or mental suffering, or placing a child in a situation where health is endangered, under circumstances likely to produce great bodily harm or death (felony) or otherwise (misdemeanor).

Full name: Sending harmful sexual matter to minors; online solicitation of minors
What it covers: Knowingly sending harmful sexual matter to a minor with intent to arouse or seduce (Cal.); using a computer service to seduce, solicit, lure, or entice a child, or transmitting sexual material to a minor (Fla.).

Full name: Stalking and electronic harassment
What it covers: Willful, malicious, repeated following or harassment with a credible threat (stalking); repeated electronic communications made with intent to annoy or harass, or obscene language with intent to annoy.

Full name: Criminal threats
What it covers: Willfully threatening a crime that would result in death or great bodily injury, intended to be taken as a threat, causing sustained reasonable fear.

Full name: Nonconsensual intimate images, incl. synthetic images
Citation: Cal. Penal Code § 647(j)(4); Va. Code Ann. § 18.2-386.2; Tex. Penal Code § 21.165
What it covers: Intentionally distributing intimate images of an identifiable person, knowing they were to remain private, causing serious emotional distress (Cal.); maliciously disseminating nude or sexual images of another with intent to coerce, harass, or intimidate, where 'another person' includes a recognizable person whose image was used to create or modify the depiction (Va., Class 1 misdemeanor); producing or distributing sexually explicit deep fake media without consent (Tex.). Effective date used here is the first of these to reach synthetic images: Virginia's 2019 amendment (2019 Va. Acts cc. 490, 515), effective July 1, 2019.

Full name: State CSAM laws covering AI-generated material
Citation: Cal. Penal Code §§ 311.1, 311.11 (as amended by A.B. 1831, 2024)
What it covers: Knowingly possessing, producing, distributing, or exhibiting matter depicting a person under 18 in sexual conduct, now expressly including digitally altered or artificial-intelligence-generated matter (Cal. Penal Code §§ 311.1, 311.11, as amended effective Jan. 1, 2025).

Full name: Online impersonation; identity theft
What it covers: Knowingly and without consent credibly impersonating another actual person online to harm, intimidate, threaten, or defraud; willfully obtaining and using another's personal identifying information for an unlawful purpose.

Full name: Theft by false pretenses; obtaining property by fraud
What it covers: Knowingly and designedly obtaining money, property, or labor from another by false or fraudulent representation or pretense.

Full name: State computer crimes
What it covers: Knowingly accessing and without permission using, altering, damaging, deleting, or destroying data, computers, or networks, or introducing a contaminant.

Full name: Unlicensed practice of medicine
Citation: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 2052; Fla. Stat. § 458.327
What it covers: Practicing, attempting to practice, or advertising or holding out as practicing medicine (diagnosing, treating, prescribing) without a valid license.

Full name: Unlicensed practice of psychology or psychotherapy
Citation: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code §§ 2903, 2970; 225 ILCS 155 (Illinois WOPR Act, civil penalties)
What it covers: Practicing psychology or holding oneself out as a psychologist without a license (California; violations of the licensing chapter are misdemeanors, up to 6 months and $2,000); providing, advertising, or offering therapy or psychotherapy, including through internet-based AI, without a licensed professional (Illinois WOPR Act, eff. Aug. 1, 2025; civil penalties).

Full name: Unauthorized practice of law
Citation: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code §§ 6125, 6126; Fla. Stat. § 454.23
What it covers: Practicing law, or advertising or holding oneself out as entitled to practice law, without being an active member of the bar.

Full name: Election deepfakes and deceptive voter suppression
Citation: Minn. Stat. § 609.771; N.H. Rev. Stat. Ann. § 659:40
What it covers: Disseminating a deepfake of a candidate without consent, knowing or recklessly disregarding that it is a deepfake, with intent to injure a candidate or influence an election, within 90 days before a nominating convention or after absentee voting starts (Minn.); knowingly attempting to deter a person from voting through fraudulent, deceptive, or misleading information, a class B felony (N.H.). The consultant behind the January 2024 AI Biden robocalls was acquitted under the N.H. statute in June 2025.

Full name: Eavesdropping and recording confidential communications without all-party consent
What it covers: Intentionally recording or eavesdropping on a confidential communication without the consent of all parties, or wiretapping or reading communications in transit without consent.

Full name: False reports of crimes and emergencies
What it covers: Knowingly reporting a false emergency that results in an emergency response, or knowingly making a false report of a crime to police.

Full name: Impersonating a police officer or public official
What it covers: Willfully wearing, exhibiting, or using the authority of a peace officer, or falsely representing oneself as one, with intent to fraudulently impersonate or deceive.

Full name: Title VII (employment discrimination, incl. disparate impact)
What it covers: Employer, employment agency, or agent refusing to hire, firing, or classifying applicants or employees because of race, color, religion, sex, or national origin, including neutral selection tools with unjustified disparate impact.

Full name: Age Discrimination in Employment Act
What it covers: Employer discrimination against applicants or employees aged 40 or older, including automatic rejection by age.
Mental state required: none for disparate impact (Smith v. City of Jackson)

Full name: ADA Title I (employment)
What it covers: Covered employers discriminating against qualified individuals with disabilities, including screening criteria that screen out disabled applicants and failure to provide reasonable accommodation in testing.

Full name: ADA Title II (state and local government)
What it covers: Public entities excluding qualified disabled people from, or denying them the benefits of, services, programs, or activities, or subjecting them to discrimination.
Mental state required: none for injunctive relief; deliberate indifference for damages in many circuits

Full name: ADA Title III (public accommodations)
What it covers: Discrimination on the basis of disability in the full and equal enjoyment of goods, services, and facilities of places of public accommodation, including screening criteria and failure to make reasonable modifications.

Full name: Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act
What it covers: Disability discrimination by any program or activity receiving federal financial assistance, or by federal executive agencies.

Full name: Fair Housing Act
What it covers: Discrimination in the sale, rental, or advertising of housing, and in residential real estate-related transactions, because of race, color, religion, sex, familial status, national origin, or disability, including ad delivery and tenant screening with discriminatory effects.

Full name: Equal Credit Opportunity Act
What it covers: Creditor discrimination in any aspect of a credit transaction on the basis of race, color, religion, national origin, sex, marital status, age, or receipt of public assistance; duty to give specific reasons for adverse action.

Full name: Fair Credit Reporting Act
What it covers: Consumer reporting agencies (including tenant and background screening vendors) failing to follow reasonable procedures for maximum possible accuracy or to reinvestigate disputes; willful or negligent noncompliance actionable.

Full name: Title VI of the Civil Rights Act
What it covers: Discrimination on the basis of race, color, or national origin in programs receiving federal financial assistance; private suits require intentional discrimination (Alexander v. Sandoval); federal disparate-impact enforcement is being rolled back.

Full name: Section 1983 (constitutional torts by state actors)
What it covers: Persons acting under color of state law depriving anyone of constitutional rights, e.g., arrest without probable cause (Fourth Amendment), benefit terminations without due process, or intentional discrimination (equal protection); municipal liability requires a policy or custom (Monell).

Full name: Section 1981 (race discrimination in contracts)
What it covers: Intentional race discrimination in making and enforcing contracts, including employment and commercial transactions.

Full name: Copyright infringement; removal of copyright management information
What it covers: Unauthorized reproduction, distribution, or derivative use of protected works; knowingly removing or altering copyright management information.

Full name: Lanham Act false endorsement and false advertising
What it covers: Use in commerce of a person's name, voice, or likeness, or false or misleading representations, likely to cause confusion about sponsorship or endorsement, or misrepresenting the nature or qualities of goods.

Full name: Telephone Consumer Protection Act; Truth in Caller ID
What it covers: Calls using an artificial or prerecorded voice without prior express consent (AI-generated voices included per FCC 2024 ruling); spoofing caller ID with intent to defraud or cause harm.

Full name: Wiretap Act and Stored Communications Act civil remedies
What it covers: Civil damages for unlawful interception, disclosure, or use of communications and unauthorized access to stored communications.

Full name: Video Privacy Protection Act
What it covers: Video service providers knowingly disclosing personally identifiable information about what a consumer watched.

Full name: False Claims Act
What it covers: Knowingly presenting or causing false claims for federal payment, or false records material to a claim (e.g., Medicare Advantage coverage decisions or billing driven by algorithms).

Full name: Securities and investment adviser antifraud (incl. AI washing)
What it covers: Material misstatements in connection with securities, and investment adviser fraud or deceptive practices, including false claims about using AI (SEC enforcement 2024).
Mental state required: scienter for 10b-5; negligence suffices for some § 206 claims

Full name: Sherman Act civil enforcement and treble damages
What it covers: Civil suits by the government or injured parties for agreements in restraint of trade, including algorithmic price coordination among competitors.

Full name: Federal civil action for disclosure of intimate images
What it covers: Civil action against a person who discloses an intimate visual depiction of an identifiable individual without consent, knowing or recklessly disregarding the lack of consent.

Full name: Civil remedy for victims of child sexual exploitation
What it covers: Civil damages for minors victimized by violations of federal child sexual exploitation statutes, including production and distribution of CSAM depicting them.

Full name: CFAA civil action
What it covers: Civil damages and injunctive relief for persons harmed by CFAA violations causing specified losses.

Full name: Fair Labor Standards Act
What it covers: Failure to pay covered US workers the minimum wage or overtime (relevant to underpaid data labeling and content moderation work done in the United States).

Full name: Negligence
Citation: Restatement (Third) of Torts: Liability for Physical and Emotional Harm §§ 3, 7
What it covers: Failure to exercise reasonable care, owed to those foreseeably endangered, causing physical or (in limited cases) emotional harm.

Full name: Negligent misrepresentation (incl. information causing physical harm)
What it covers: Negligently giving false information that another reasonably relies on, causing physical harm (§ 311) or pecuniary loss in a business transaction (§ 552); e.g., a company's agent misstating a refund policy.

Full name: Product liability: design defect and failure to warn
Citation: Restatement (Third) of Torts: Products Liability §§ 1, 2; Garcia v. Character Technologies, Inc., 785 F. Supp. 3d 1157 (M.D. Fla. 2025)
What it covers: Commercial sellers are liable for harm from products defective in design (a reasonable alternative design would have reduced foreseeable risk) or lacking adequate warnings. In Garcia the court treated the Character.AI app as a product for claims arising from design defects (no age verification, humanlike design, no way to exclude indecent content), declined at the pleading stage to hold the chatbot's output is protected speech, and let the product claims proceed.

Full name: Wrongful death and survival actions
Citation: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 377.60; Fla. Stat. §§ 768.16-.26
What it covers: Statutory action by survivors for a death caused by the wrongful act or neglect of another.

Full name: Defamation (libel and slander)
Citation: Restatement (Second) of Torts § 558; Walters v. OpenAI, L.L.C., No. 23-A-04860-2 (Ga. Super. Ct. Gwinnett Cnty. May 19, 2025)
What it covers: Publication to a third party of a false and defamatory statement of fact about an identifiable person, with the required fault and damages. In the first chatbot defamation case the court granted OpenAI summary judgment: no defamatory meaning given the context and disclaimers, no proof of negligence or actual malice, and no damages.
Mental state required: negligence (private figures) or actual malice (public figures)

Full name: Intentional or negligent infliction of emotional distress
What it covers: Extreme and outrageous conduct intentionally or recklessly causing severe emotional distress (negligent infliction recognized in narrower forms).

Full name: Invasion of privacy torts
What it covers: Intrusion upon seclusion, public disclosure of private facts, false light, and appropriation of name or likeness.

Full name: Statutory right of publicity (name, likeness, voice)
Citation: Cal. Civ. Code § 3344; Tenn. Code Ann. §§ 47-25-1101 to -1108 (ELVIS Act, eff. July 1, 2024)
What it covers: Knowing use of another's name, voice, signature, photograph, or likeness for advertising or commercial purposes without consent; Tennessee's ELVIS Act expressly reaches voice simulations and the distribution of tools whose primary purpose is producing a person's voice or likeness without authorization.

Full name: Illinois Biometric Information Privacy Act
What it covers: Collecting, capturing, or obtaining biometric identifiers (faceprints, voiceprints) without written notice and release, profiting from biometric data, or lacking a retention policy; private right of action with liquidated damages.
Mental state required: none (higher damages for intentional or reckless)

Full name: California Consumer Privacy Act / CPRA
What it covers: Notice, access, deletion, opt-out, and sensitive-data limits on personal information collected by covered businesses; private action limited to data breaches (§ 1798.150); agency and AG enforcement otherwise.

Full name: State unfair and deceptive practices laws
Citation: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code §§ 17200, 17500; Fla. Stat. § 501.204; Tex. Bus. & Com. Code § 17.46
What it covers: Unlawful, unfair, or fraudulent business acts and false or misleading advertising, enforced by attorneys general and, in most states, private plaintiffs.

Full name: State anti-discrimination statutes
Citation: Cal. Gov. Code § 12940 (FEHA); Cal. Civ. Code § 51 (Unruh Act); N.Y. Exec. Law § 296
What it covers: Discrimination in employment, housing, and business establishments on protected characteristics, often broader than federal law (more classes, smaller employers, lower intent requirements).

Full name: Civil fraud and deceit
What it covers: Willful deception with intent to induce reliance, including suggestion of a falsehood, suppression of a fact, or a promise made without intent to perform.

Full name: Breach of contract and warranty
What it covers: Failure to perform promises, including affirmations of fact about goods (express warranty) and goods unfit for ordinary purposes (implied warranty), and representations a company's agent makes to customers.

Full name: False arrest, false imprisonment, malicious prosecution
What it covers: Intentional confinement without lawful privilege, and initiating proceedings without probable cause and with malice that end in the accused's favor.

Full name: California Invasion of Privacy Act civil action
What it covers: Civil damages ($5,000 per violation or treble actual damages) for violations of California's wiretapping and recording statutes, used against AI call-recording and chat-interception tools.

Full name: Civil action for sexually explicit digitized depictions
What it covers: Civil action against a person who creates and intentionally discloses, or intentionally discloses, sexually explicit material depicting an identifiable person (including digitized depictions) without consent.

Full name: Professional negligence (medical, legal, other licensed professions)
Citation: Common law; e.g., Cal. Civ. Code § 3333.2 (medical damages cap)
What it covers: A professional's failure to meet the standard of care of the profession, causing harm (incl. diagnosis, treatment, and legal advice errors).

Full name: Trespass to chattels and conversion
What it covers: Intentional interference with another's personal property, including computer systems and data, causing harm (trespass) or so serious it warrants full value (conversion).

Full name: California companion chatbot law (SB 243)
What it covers: Operators of companion chatbot platforms must notify users the bot is artificial when a reasonable person could be misled; may not let a companion chatbot engage users without a protocol to prevent suicidal ideation, suicide, or self-harm content and refer users to crisis services; must stop sexual content with known minors; annual reporting to the Office of Suicide Prevention from July 1, 2027; private right of action.

Full name: New York AI companion models law
What it covers: Unlawful to operate or provide an AI companion without a protocol to detect and address user expressions of suicidal ideation or self-harm, including referral to crisis services such as 988; required notices that the user is not talking to a human; Attorney General enforcement with civil penalties.

Full name: Illinois Wellness and Oversight for Psychological Resources Act
What it covers: No individual, corporation, or entity may provide, advertise, or offer therapy or psychotherapy in Illinois, including through internet-based AI, unless conducted by a licensed professional; licensed professionals may use AI only for administrative and supplementary support, not independent therapeutic decisions; civil penalties up to $10,000 per violation.

Full name: Texas Responsible Artificial Intelligence Governance Act
Citation: Tex. Bus. & Com. Code ch. 552 (Texas Responsible Artificial Intelligence Governance Act, H.B. 149 (2025)), e.g., § 552.052
What it covers: Bars developing or deploying an AI system in a manner that intentionally aims to incite or encourage a person to commit self-harm (including suicide), harm another person, or engage in criminal activity; separate prohibitions on unlawful sexual deepfakes, intentional discrimination, and certain government uses; enforced by the Texas Attorney General.

Full name: Colorado automated decision-making technology law (SB 26-189, replacing the 2024 Colorado AI Act)
Citation: Colo. S.B. 26-189 (2026), repealing and reenacting S.B. 24-205
What it covers: The 2024 Colorado AI Act's duty of care against algorithmic discrimination never took effect: it was repealed and replaced on May 14, 2026 by a narrower notice, disclosure, and recordkeeping regime for automated decision-making technology used in consequential decisions, effective January 1, 2027.

Full name: New York City automated employment decision tool law (Local Law 144)
What it covers: Employers and agencies using automated employment decision tools for NYC jobs must obtain an annual independent bias audit, publish results, and notify candidates.

Full name: Illinois Artificial Intelligence Video Interview Act; IHRA AI amendment
What it covers: Employers using AI to analyze video interviews must give notice, explain the AI, and obtain consent; from 2026 the Illinois Human Rights Act bars employer use of AI that has a discriminatory effect or uses zip codes as a proxy.

Full name: California bot disclosure law
What it covers: Unlawful to use a bot to communicate with a person in California with intent to mislead them about its artificial identity to incentivize a sale or influence an election vote, unless clearly disclosed.

Full name: Utah AI disclosure and mental health chatbot laws
Citation: Utah Code Ann. §§ 13-77-103 (generative AI disclosure), 13-72a-101 to -201 (mental health chatbots)
What it covers: Businesses must disclose that a consumer is interacting with generative AI and not a human when asked, and prominently up front in high-risk interactions in regulated occupations; suppliers of mental health chatbots may not sell or share users' health information or inputs and face advertising and disclosure limits.

Full name: TAKE IT DOWN Act notice-and-removal duty
What it covers: Covered platforms had until May 19, 2026 to set up a process for identifiable people to request removal of nonconsensual intimate images and digital forgeries, and must remove the image and known identical copies within 48 hours of a valid request; enforced by the FTC.

Full name: FTC Act section 5 (unfair or deceptive acts)
What it covers: Unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce, including false claims about AI capabilities and unfair deployment of inaccurate facial recognition (the FTC's December 2023 order barred Rite Aid from using facial recognition for five years); remedies include orders and deletion of models and data.

Full name: Children's Online Privacy Protection Act and Rule
What it covers: Operators of child-directed services, or with actual knowledge of users under 13, must give notice and get verifiable parental consent before collecting children's personal information (incl. voice recordings), and limit retention; civil penalties.

Full name: FDA medical device premarket review (incl. software as a medical device)
What it covers: Software intended to diagnose, treat, or prevent disease is a device requiring classification and, as applicable, 510(k) clearance, De Novo, or premarket approval before marketing.

Full name: Motor vehicle safety standards, defect recalls, crash reporting
What it covers: Vehicles and equipment must meet safety standards; manufacturers must notify and remedy safety defects (incl. driver-assistance software) and report crashes involving automated driving systems and Level 2 ADAS; civil penalties.

Full name: FAA aircraft certification and operating rules
What it covers: Type and airworthiness certification of aircraft systems (incl. automated flight control software) and rules for unmanned aircraft operations.

Full name: OSHA general duty clause and machine guarding
What it covers: Employers must keep workplaces free of recognized hazards likely to cause death or serious harm, including guarding of robots and automated machinery.

Full name: Medicare Advantage coverage criteria rule
What it covers: Medicare Advantage organizations must base medical necessity determinations on Medicare coverage criteria, whether care is reasonable and necessary, and the enrollee's own medical history, physician recommendations, and clinical notes, with medical director involvement where appropriate; they may not deny basic benefits on criteria not in the rule.

Full name: HIPAA Privacy and Security Rules
What it covers: Covered entities and business associates may use and disclose protected health information only as permitted, with safeguards and breach notification.

Full name: Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act
What it covers: Schools receiving federal funds may not disclose personally identifiable information from student education records without consent, except as permitted.

Full name: Uniform Guidelines on Employee Selection Procedures
What it covers: Employers must monitor selection procedures (incl. automated tools) for adverse impact (four-fifths rule) and validate procedures that have it.

Full name: Regulation B adverse action notices
What it covers: Creditors must give applicants a statement of the specific reasons for adverse credit actions, whatever decision method they use.

Full name: FCC ruling that AI-generated voices are 'artificial' under the TCPA
What it covers: Calls using AI-generated or cloned voices are 'artificial' voice calls under the TCPA and need prior express consent like other artificial or prerecorded calls; the FCC fined the consultant behind the January 2024 New Hampshire Biden robocalls $6 million in September 2024.

Full name: SEC market access rule and trading controls
What it covers: Broker-dealers with market access must maintain risk controls to prevent erroneous orders and runaway algorithms (applied after the 2012 Knight Capital loss).

Full name: Court sanctions and professional conduct rules
Citation: Fed. R. Civ. P. 11(b); ABA Model Rules of Prof'l Conduct 1.1, 3.3 (as adopted by states); Mata v. Avianca, Inc. (S.D.N.Y. June 22, 2023)
What it covers: Attorneys certify that legal contentions are warranted by existing law after reasonable inquiry, owe competence and candor to the tribunal; sanctions for fabricated citations (Mata v. Avianca, S.D.N.Y. 2023).

Full name: Consumer Product Safety Act reporting and recall
What it covers: Manufacturers and sellers must report products that contain defects creating substantial product hazards or unreasonable risks of serious injury, and recall them; civil penalties.

Full name: Consumer Financial Protection Act UDAAP
What it covers: Unfair, deceptive, or abusive acts or practices by providers of consumer financial products and services, including customer-service systems that obstruct consumers.

Full name: Respondeat superior and agency
What it covers: An employer is subject to vicarious liability for torts committed by employees acting within the scope of employment; principals are bound by agents' acts within actual or apparent authority.

Full name: Corporate criminal liability for agents' acts
Citation: New York Central & Hudson River R.R. Co. v. United States, 212 U.S. 481 (1909)
What it covers: A corporation may be held criminally liable for crimes committed by its agents acting within the scope of their employment.

Full name: Responsible corporate officer doctrine
What it covers: Corporate officers with responsibility and authority to prevent or correct a public-welfare violation (FDCA) may be criminally liable without personal knowledge or participation.

Full name: AI vendor as employer's agent under anti-discrimination law
Citation: Mobley v. Workday, Inc., 740 F. Supp. 3d 796 (N.D. Cal. 2024)
What it covers: An AI screening vendor to which employers delegate traditional hiring functions (rejecting applicants, recommending who advances) plausibly qualifies as the employers' agent, and so an 'employer,' under Title VII, the ADEA, and the ADA. The court: nothing in the federal anti-discrimination statutes distinguishes between delegating functions to an automated agent versus a live human one.

Full name: Section 230 immunity
What it covers: No provider of an interactive computer service shall be treated as publisher or speaker of information provided by another information content provider. An information content provider is any person or entity responsible, in whole or in part, for the creation or development of the information, so a company that generates the content itself is not shielded for it.

Full name: Proving discriminatory intent from statements plus disparate outcomes
Citation: Village of Arlington Heights v. Metro. Hous. Dev. Corp., 429 U.S. 252, 265-68 (1977) (government actors); Int'l Bhd. of Teamsters v. United States, 431 U.S. 324, 336-40 (1977) (private employers); 42 U.S.C. § 1981a(a)
What it covers: Intent may be proved circumstantially. For government action, Arlington Heights looks to disparate impact, historical background, sequence of events, departures from normal procedure, and contemporaneous statements by decisionmakers. For private employers, Teamsters allows gross statistical disparities bolstered by evidence of specific discrimination to prove a pattern or practice of intentional discrimination. Coding rule: discriminatory statements put out by a company or its own system, paired with exclusion in a covered domain (employment, housing, credit, public accommodation, government programs), count as evidence of intent, moving intent-required claims to 'yes, if facts are proven.' Intentional discrimination opens compensatory and punitive damages under 42 U.S.C. § 1981a (Title VII expressly excludes disparate impact; the ADA clause's wording is less tidy).

Full name: Discriminatory statements within covered transactions are not protected speech
Citation: 42 U.S.C. § 2000e-3(b); 42 U.S.C. § 3604(c); Pittsburgh Press Co. v. Pittsburgh Comm'n on Human Relations, 413 U.S. 376, 388-89 (1973); N.Y. Civ. Rights Law § 40
What it covers: A company's notices, statements, or advertisements indicating a preference, limitation, or discrimination on a protected basis in employment or housing are unlawful in themselves, with no denied applicant required; commercial speech proposing illegal discrimination has no First Amendment protection. State public accommodations laws (e.g., New York) bar a business from declaring a protected group's patronage unwelcome. Coding rule: test a company's or its deployed system's discriminatory statements to its own customers, applicants, tenants, or workers under these provisions before treating them as protected speech. Offensive speech to the public at large, outside any covered relationship, remains protected.

Full name: Admiralty and maritime claims; in rem actions against a vessel
Citation: Fed. R. Civ. P. Supp. R. A, C, E; general maritime law
What it covers: Admiralty claims, including actions in rem against the vessel itself to enforce a maritime lien, where the vessel is the named defendant and is arrested as security. Relevant to incidents involving autonomous or remotely operated vessels and to the personhood question, since admiralty already proceeds against a thing.

Full name: Title IX (sex discrimination in federally funded education)
Citation: 20 U.S.C. § 1681(a); Gebser v. Lago Vista Indep. Sch. Dist., 524 U.S. 274, 290 (1998)
What it covers: No person may, on the basis of sex, be excluded from, denied the benefits of, or subjected to discrimination under any education program or activity receiving federal financial assistance. For damages based on a teacher's harassment that does not involve official policy, an official with authority to take corrective action must have had actual knowledge and responded with deliberate indifference (Gebser).
Mental state required: intentional discrimination or deliberate indifference for damages

Full name: ACA section 1557 (discrimination in health programs)
What it covers: Discrimination on grounds prohibited by Title VI (race, color, national origin), Title IX (sex), the Age Discrimination Act (age), or Section 504 (disability) in any health program or activity any part of which receives federal financial assistance, or that an executive agency or an ACA Title I entity administers.

Full name: Section 1557 rule on patient care decision support tools
What it covers: Covered health entities may not discriminate on the basis of race, color, national origin, sex, age, or disability through patient care decision support tools, including algorithms, and must make reasonable efforts to identify tools that use those characteristics as inputs and to mitigate the risk of discrimination from their use.
Mental state required: none required for the duty; reasonable efforts standard

Full name: Title II of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 (public accommodations)
What it covers: Full and equal enjoyment of the goods, services, facilities, and accommodations of any place of public accommodation without discrimination or segregation on the ground of race, color, religion, or national origin. Covered places are listed establishments serving the public: lodgings, restaurants and other facilities selling food for consumption on the premises, gasoline stations, and places of exhibition or entertainment such as theaters and stadiums. The remedy is a civil action for preventive relief (injunction).

Full name: Age Discrimination Act of 1975
What it covers: No person may, on the basis of age, be excluded from participation in, denied the benefits of, or subjected to discrimination under any program or activity receiving federal financial assistance; private suits may seek to enjoin violations.

Full name: Section 508 (federal electronic and information technology)
What it covers: Federal departments and agencies that develop, procure, maintain, or use electronic and information technology must give disabled federal employees and disabled members of the public access comparable to others, unless an undue burden; disabled individuals may file complaints, with the remedies of 29 U.S.C. § 794a(a)(2) and (b).

Full name: Twenty-First Century Communications and Video Accessibility Act
What it covers: Providers of advanced communications services and manufacturers of equipment used for them must make those services and equipment accessible to and usable by disabled people unless not achievable; the FCC receives and adjudicates complaints.

Full name: Individuals with Disabilities Education Act
What it covers: States receiving IDEA funds must make a free appropriate public education available to all children with disabilities ages 3 through 21, with procedural safeguards, due process hearings, and a right to bring a civil action after the administrative hearing.

Full name: Air Carrier Access Act
Citation: 49 U.S.C. § 41705(a); Love v. Delta Air Lines, 310 F.3d 1347, 1358-59 (11th Cir. 2002)
What it covers: Air carriers, including foreign air carriers, may not discriminate against an otherwise qualified disabled individual in providing air transportation. Enforced by the Department of Transportation; the Eleventh Circuit holds there is no implied private right of action in district court (Love).

Full name: Conspiracy to deprive of equal protection
What it covers: Two or more persons conspiring to deprive any person or class of persons of the equal protection of the laws or equal privileges and immunities. Reaches private conspiracies, but requires some racial, or perhaps otherwise class-based, invidiously discriminatory animus (Griffin).

Full name: Equal Pay Act
What it covers: Employers may not pay employees of one sex less than employees of the opposite sex in the same establishment for equal work requiring equal skill, effort, and responsibility under similar working conditions, except under a seniority system, a merit system, a system measuring earnings by quantity or quality of production, or a factor other than sex.

Full name: Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act, Title II
What it covers: Employers may not discriminate against employees because of genetic information, or request, require, or purchase genetic information about employees or their family members, subject to narrow exceptions.

Full name: Pregnancy Discrimination Act
What it covers: Title VII's 'because of sex' includes pregnancy, childbirth, or related medical conditions, and pregnant workers must be treated the same for all employment-related purposes as others similar in their ability or inability to work.

Full name: Pregnant Workers Fairness Act
What it covers: Covered employers must make reasonable accommodations to the known limitations related to pregnancy, childbirth, or related medical conditions of a qualified employee absent undue hardship, and may not require an accommodation not arrived at through the interactive process, deny opportunities, or take adverse action because of the need for or request for accommodation.
Mental state required: none required for failure to accommodate

Full name: Voting Rights Act section 11(b) (voter intimidation)
Citation: 52 U.S.C. § 10307(b); Nat'l Coal. on Black Civic Participation v. Wohl, 498 F. Supp. 3d 457, 476 (S.D.N.Y. 2020)
What it covers: No person, whether acting under color of law or otherwise, may intimidate, threaten, or coerce, or attempt to, any person for voting or attempting to vote. Private parties may sue, and robocalls spreading false threats about the consequences of voting by mail were found likely to violate the section at the temporary restraining order stage (Wohl).

Full name: California Unruh Civil Rights Act and Disabled Persons Act
Citation: Cal. Civ. Code §§ 51(b), (f), 52(a), 54.1, 54.3; Munson v. Del Taco, Inc., 46 Cal. 4th 661, 670 (2009)
What it covers: All persons, regardless of sex, race, color, religion, ancestry, national origin, disability, medical condition, genetic information, marital status, sexual orientation, citizenship, primary language, or immigration status, are entitled to full and equal accommodations in all business establishments of every kind. Any ADA violation is also an Unruh violation (§ 51(f)) and a Disabled Persons Act violation (§ 54.1(d)). Damages of at least $4,000 per offense (§ 52(a)) or $1,000 (§ 54.3); ADA-based Unruh damages require no proof of intentional discrimination (Munson).
Mental state required: intent generally; none for ADA-based claims

Full name: California Ralph and Bane Civil Rights Acts
What it covers: Right to be free from violence, or intimidation by threat of violence, because of political affiliation, a characteristic listed in § 51 (including religion and disability), or labor-dispute position; actual and exemplary damages and a $25,000 civil penalty (§ 52(b)). Speech alone supports a Ralph claim only if it threatens violence against a specific person or group who reasonably fears it, with reckless disregard and apparent ability. The Bane Act reaches interference or attempted interference, by threat, intimidation, or coercion, with constitutional or statutory rights (§ 52.1).

Full name: California sexual harassment in business relationships
What it covers: Liability for sexual advances, requests, or other conduct of a sexual nature or hostile nature based on gender, unwelcome and pervasive or severe, within a business, service, or professional relationship (or where the defendant holds itself out as able to help establish one), causing economic loss, personal injury, or emotional distress; remedies under § 52(b).
Mental state required: none stated beyond unwelcome severe or pervasive conduct

Full name: Shepard-Byrd Hate Crimes Prevention Act
What it covers: Willfully causing bodily injury, or attempting to through fire, a firearm, a dangerous weapon, or an explosive or incendiary device, because of actual or perceived race, color, religion, or national origin ((a)(1)), or religion, national origin, gender, sexual orientation, gender identity, or disability with a commerce nexus ((a)(2)).
Mental state required: willfully; because of the protected characteristic

Full name: California hate crime (interference with civil rights)
What it covers: By force or threat of force, willfully injuring, intimidating, interfering with, oppressing, or threatening any person in the free exercise of a constitutional or statutory right because of actual or perceived disability, gender, nationality, race or ethnicity, religion, sexual orientation, or association with such a person or group.

Full name: Damage to religious property; obstruction of free exercise
What it covers: Intentionally defacing, damaging, or destroying religious real property because of its religious character, or intentionally obstructing by force or threat of force (including threats against religious property) any person's free exercise of religious beliefs, in or affecting interstate commerce; also damaging religious property because of the race, color, or ethnic characteristics of people associated with it.

Full name: ADA Title II web and mobile app accessibility rule
What it covers: State and local governments' web content and mobile apps, including those provided through contractors, must conform to WCAG 2.1 Level A and AA beginning April 26, 2027 for public entities of 50,000 or more people and April 26, 2028 for smaller entities and special districts, subject to fundamental-alteration and undue-burden limits.

Full name: Religious beliefs cannot be tried for truth (United States v. Ballard)
What it covers: The truth or falsity of religious doctrines or beliefs may not be submitted to a jury; in Ballard the jury decided only whether the defendants believed their representations in good faith. Coding use: a fraud or misrepresentation theory cannot rest on the falsity of a religious claim (for example, a system telling a user he is divine); product, negligence, and duty-to-vulnerable-user theories do not depend on religious truth.

Full name: No duty of nontherapist counselors to refer suicidal counselees (Nally)
Citation: Nally v. Grace Community Church, 47 Cal. 3d 278, 299-300 (1988)
What it covers: No duty to prevent suicide or refer to professional help is imposed on a nontherapist counselor who counsels a potentially suicidal person on secular or spiritual matters, including pastoral counselors; the court left open liability for nontherapist counselors who hold themselves out as professionals. Midpage flags Brown v. USA Taekwondo, 11 Cal. 5th 204 (2021), as limiting Nally's reach without overruling it.

Full name: Undue influence and financial elder abuse (California)
Citation: Cal. Civ. Code § 1575; Cal. Welf. & Inst. Code §§ 15610.30, 15657.5
What it covers: Undue influence is the use of a confidence reposed in one, or real or apparent authority, to obtain an unfair advantage; taking unfair advantage of another's weakness of mind; or taking grossly oppressive advantage of another's necessities or distress (§ 1575). Financial abuse of an elder or dependent adult includes taking, or assisting in taking, property for a wrongful use, with intent to defraud, or by undue influence, with mandatory attorney's fees when proven (Welf. & Inst. Code §§ 15610.30, 15657.5).
Mental state required: intent to defraud or wrongful use; or undue influence

Full name: Fortune telling for a fee (New York)
What it covers: For a fee or compensation, claiming or pretending to tell fortunes, or holding oneself out as able, by claimed or pretended use of occult powers, to answer questions or give advice on personal matters or to exorcise, influence, or affect evil spirits or curses. Does not apply to a show or exhibition solely for entertainment or amusement. Class B misdemeanor.

Full name: Ancestry and ethnic discrimination under §§ 1981 and 1982
Citation: Saint Francis Coll. v. Al-Khazraji, 481 U.S. 604, 613 (1987); Shaare Tefila Congregation v. Cobb, 481 U.S. 615, 617-18 (1987)
What it covers: 42 U.S.C. §§ 1981 and 1982 reach intentional discrimination against identifiable classes because of ancestry or ethnic characteristics, including Arabs and Jews, whether or not modern classifications would call it racial; discrimination based solely on place of origin or religion is not covered. Coding use: ancestry-based discrimination against Jewish, Arab, or other ethnic groups in contracting or property is coded under VF-1981.

Full name: Federal Tort Claims Act
What it covers: The United States is liable for injury or death caused by the negligent or wrongful act or omission of a federal employee acting within the scope of employment where a private person would be liable under the law of the place, in the same manner and to the same extent as a private individual under like circumstances (no prejudgment interest or punitive damages). An administrative claim must come first. Excludes discretionary functions and most intentional torts, but assault, battery, false imprisonment, false arrest, abuse of process, and malicious prosecution claims are allowed for acts of investigative or law enforcement officers. The private-person standard is the statute's own human-substitution test.

Full name: Administrative Procedure Act review
What it covers: A person suffering legal wrong because of agency action may obtain judicial review seeking relief other than money damages; courts set aside agency action that is arbitrary, capricious, an abuse of discretion, or otherwise not in accordance with law, or contrary to constitutional right, including Fifth Amendment equal protection.

Full name: Privacy Act of 1974 (accuracy of agency records)
What it covers: Federal agencies must maintain records used in determinations about individuals with the accuracy, relevance, timeliness, and completeness reasonably necessary to assure fairness; an individual harmed by an adverse determination based on such a record may sue, recovering actual damages (at least $1,000) and fees when the agency acted intentionally or willfully.

Full name: California Government Claims Act
What it covers: A public entity is liable only as provided by statute; it is vicariously liable for an employee's act or omission within the scope of employment that would give rise to a cause of action against the employee, but not where the employee is immune, including for discretionary acts; a written claim must be presented and acted on before a suit for money damages.

Full name: Limits on damages suits against federal officers (Bivens)
What it covers: Extending a Bivens damages action to a new context is a disfavored judicial activity; no Bivens action lies if there is any rational reason to think Congress is better suited to weigh creating a damages remedy, which the Court says will be true in most every case.

Full name: First Step Act risk and needs assessment system
What it covers: The Attorney General must develop and publicly release a risk and needs assessment system for federal prisoners, and annually review, validate, and publish it, including statistical validation of its tools and an evaluation of recidivism rates among similarly classified prisoners to identify unwarranted disparities among demographic groups, revising the system to address any identified disparities.

Full name: No discrimination in immigrant visa issuance
What it covers: Except as specified, no person shall receive any preference or priority or be discriminated against in the issuance of an immigrant visa because of race, sex, nationality, place of birth, or place of residence.

Full name: Limitation of Liability Act (shipowners)
What it covers: A vessel owner's liability for claims arising without the owner's privity or knowledge (cargo loss, collision, and other listed claims) is capped at the value of the vessel and pending freight; the owner may file a limitation action within six months after written notice of a claim. An existing statutory liability cap that attaches through a thing and gives way where the owner had privity or knowledge.
Mental state required: n/a; cap lost on owner's privity or knowledge

Full name: Jones Act (injured seamen)
What it covers: A seaman injured in the course of employment, or the personal representative after death, may elect to sue the employer at law with a jury; the laws governing recovery for personal injury or death of railway employees apply.

Full name: Suits in Admiralty Act and Public Vessels Act
What it covers: Where a civil action in admiralty could be maintained if the vessel were privately owned or operated, an admiralty action in personam may be brought against the United States; a civil action in personam in admiralty lies against the United States for damages caused by a public vessel of the United States.

Full name: Violence against maritime navigation; false maritime threats
What it covers: Unlawfully and intentionally seizing control of a ship by force, threat, or intimidation, or destroying or damaging a ship or its cargo in a way likely to endanger safe navigation (§ 2280); imparting false information, knowing it false, about an attempt to commit such an offense, a civil penalty up to $5,000, and a crime when done knowingly, intentionally, maliciously, or with reckless disregard for human life (§ 2292).

Full name: Inland Navigation Rules: proper look-out (Rule 5)
What it covers: Every vessel must at all times maintain a proper look-out by sight and hearing and all available means appropriate in the circumstances to make a full appraisal of the situation and the risk of collision; applies to unmanned and remotely operated vessels.

Full name: Fair Debt Collection Practices Act
What it covers: Debt collectors may not engage in conduct whose natural consequence is to harass, oppress, or abuse any person, or use false, deceptive, or misleading representations, in collecting debts; actual damages plus statutory damages up to $1,000 and fees.
Mental state required: none required (strict liability with bona fide error defense)

Full name: Electronic Fund Transfer Act and Regulation E
What it covers: A consumer's liability for unauthorized electronic fund transfers is capped (the lesser of $50 or the amount transferred with notice within two business days of learning of a lost or stolen access device; up to $500 with later notice; more for failing to report statement errors); financial institutions must investigate reported errors; violators are civilly liable.

Full name: Truth in Lending Act: unauthorized card use and civil liability
What it covers: A cardholder is liable for unauthorized use of a credit card only up to $50 and only if statutory conditions are met; creditors failing to comply with TILA requirements are civilly liable.

Full name: Insurance bad faith (implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing)
Citation: Gruenberg v. Aetna Ins. Co., 9 Cal. 3d 566, 575-76 (1973)
What it covers: Every insurance contract carries an implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing; an insurer that unreasonably and in bad faith withholds payment of its insured's claim is liable in tort. Displaced for employer-sponsored plans by ERISA (see VF-ERISA).

Full name: Unfair claims settlement practices (California)
Citation: Cal. Ins. Code § 790.03(h); Moradi-Shalal v. Fireman's Fund Ins. Cos., 46 Cal. 3d 287, 304 (1988)
What it covers: Knowingly committing, or committing with such frequency as to indicate a general business practice, unfair claims settlement practices, including misrepresenting pertinent facts or policy provisions, failing to adopt reasonable standards for prompt investigation and processing of claims, and not attempting in good faith to settle claims where liability is reasonably clear. Enforced by the Insurance Commissioner; no private cause of action (Moradi-Shalal).
Mental state required: knowingly, or as a general business practice

Full name: ERISA benefit claims, fiduciary duties, and preemption
What it covers: Plan fiduciaries must act solely in participants' interest with the care, skill, prudence, and diligence of a prudent person; participants may sue to recover benefits due under the plan. ERISA supersedes state laws relating to employee benefit plans, and state common-law bad-faith claims for improper processing of benefit claims are preempted, leaving ERISA's civil enforcement scheme exclusive (Pilot Life).

Full name: National Labor Relations Act unfair labor practices
What it covers: Employers may not interfere with, restrain, or coerce employees in exercising their rights to organize and engage in concerted activity, or discriminate in hire, tenure, or any term or condition of employment to encourage or discourage union membership; enforced through NLRB unfair labor practice proceedings.

Full name: Suits on collective bargaining agreements (LMRA § 301)
What it covers: Suits for violation of contracts between an employer and a labor organization may be brought in federal district court; the vehicle for enforcing collective bargaining terms on automation or AI.

Full name: Family and Medical Leave Act interference and retaliation
What it covers: Employers may not interfere with, restrain, or deny the exercise of FMLA rights, or discharge or discriminate against anyone for opposing unlawful practices; employees may sue for damages and equitable relief.
Mental state required: none for interference; motive for retaliation

Full name: California warehouse quota law (A.B. 701)
What it covers: Covered warehouse employers must give each employee a written description of each quota (tasks or materials, time period, and possible adverse action) and may not require quotas that prevent compliance with meal or rest periods, bathroom use including travel time, or occupational health and safety laws.

Full name: State timely wage payment laws
Citation: Cal. Lab. Code § 204(a); N.Y. Lab. Law § 191
What it covers: Earned wages are due on regular paydays (twice monthly in California; weekly for manual workers in New York). Coding use: earned incentive pay withheld on the basis of an automated finding.

Full name: New York employer electronic monitoring notice
Citation: N.Y. Civ. Rights Law § 52-c (second section so numbered)
What it covers: Employers with a place of business in New York that monitor or intercept employees' telephone, email, or internet access or usage by electronic means must give prior written notice upon hiring, acknowledged by the employee.

Full name: Workers' compensation exclusivity
What it covers: Where the conditions of compensation concur, workers' compensation is the employee's sole and exclusive remedy against the employer, subject to exceptions in §§ 3602, 3706, and 4558; the bar runs only against the employer.

Full name: California whistleblower retaliation
What it covers: Employers may not retaliate against employees for disclosing to a government or law enforcement agency, a supervisor, or a public body information the employee reasonably believes discloses a violation of law, whether or not disclosure is part of the job.

Full name: Predictive scheduling (Oregon)
What it covers: Covered employers must give good-faith estimates of work schedules, provide advance notice of schedules, allow rest between shifts, and pay for employer-initiated schedule changes; BOLI enforcement and civil actions for retaliation (§ 653.480).

Full name: California Investigative Consumer Reporting Agencies Act
What it covers: Investigative consumer reporting agencies and users that fail to comply with the Act are liable for actual damages or $10,000 (outside class actions), whichever is greater, plus fees, and punitive damages for grossly negligent or willful violations.

Full name: Anti-Terrorism Act civil remedy (JASTA aiding and abetting)
What it covers: US nationals injured by an act of international terrorism may recover threefold damages and fees; for acts committed, planned, or authorized by a designated foreign terrorist organization, liability extends to anyone who aids and abets by knowingly providing substantial assistance, or conspires with the person who committed the act.
Mental state required: knowing substantial assistance for secondary liability

Full name: Export Control Reform Act and Export Administration Regulations
What it covers: Willfully violating, attempting or conspiring to violate, or causing a violation of the Act or the EAR, including licensing requirements for controlled items such as advanced computing chips (ECCN 3A090), is a crime punishable by up to $1,000,000 and 20 years; civil penalties also apply.

Full name: Arms Export Control Act and ITAR
What it covers: Defense articles and defense services designated by the President may not be exported or imported without a license; defense services include assistance or training to foreign persons in the design, development, production, operation, or use of defense articles and furnishing controlled technical data; willful violations are crimes.

Full name: War Crimes Act
What it covers: Committing a war crime (grave breaches of the Geneva Conventions, listed Hague Convention violations, grave breaches of Common Article 3, and others), inside or outside the United States, where the perpetrator or victim is a US service member or national, or the offender is present in the United States.

Full name: Foreign Agents Registration Act
What it covers: Acting as an agent of a foreign principal without filing a registration statement with the Attorney General, or distributing informational materials without the required conspicuous statement that they are distributed on behalf of the foreign principal; willful violations are crimes.

Full name: Acting as an unregistered agent of a foreign government
What it covers: Acting in the United States as an agent of a foreign government without prior notification to the Attorney General, other than diplomatic and consular officers and other excepted persons.

Full name: Sanctions violations (IEEPA)
What it covers: Willfully violating, attempting or conspiring to violate, or causing a violation of a license, order, regulation, or prohibition issued under IEEPA, including economic sanctions programs.

Full name: Money laundering
What it covers: Conducting a financial transaction with proceeds of specified unlawful activity, knowing they are proceeds of unlawful activity, with intent to promote the activity or to conceal the proceeds (§ 1956); knowingly engaging in a monetary transaction over $10,000 in criminally derived property (§ 1957).

Full name: Bankruptcy fraud
What it covers: Having devised a scheme to defraud, and to execute or conceal it, filing a bankruptcy petition or document, or making a false or fraudulent representation, claim, or promise concerning a bankruptcy proceeding.

Full name: Counterfeiting United States obligations
What it covers: With intent to defraud, falsely making, forging, counterfeiting, or altering any obligation or other security of the United States, including currency.

Full name: Misuse of federal badges, names, and seals
What it covers: Manufacturing, selling, or possessing a federal badge, identification card, or other insignia of a department's prescribed design, or a likeness of one, without authorization (§ 701); using the names or initials § 709 lists (FBI, Secret Service, U.S. Mint, DEA, U.S. Marshals Service) in an advertisement or production in a manner reasonably calculated to convey federal approval, or using terms such as 'Federal', 'national', or 'Deposit Insurance' in a banking or financial business name (§ 709); knowingly displaying the Great Seal or the seals of the President, Vice President, Senate, House, or Congress to convey a false impression of government sponsorship or approval (§ 713). Names of other agencies (IRS, Postal Service, benefits agencies) are outside § 709.
Mental state required: knowingly or with purpose to mislead

Full name: Forgery (New York and California)
Citation: N.Y. Penal Law § 170.10; Cal. Penal Code § 470(a), (d)
What it covers: With intent to defraud, deceive, or injure, falsely making, completing, or altering a written instrument such as a contract, commercial instrument, credit card, public record, or official filing (N.Y. second-degree forgery); with intent to defraud, signing another's or a fictitious name to listed instruments, or falsely making, altering, or passing as genuine listed instruments, including receipts for money or goods (Cal.).

Full name: Obstruction of justice and falsification of records
What it covers: Corruptly influencing, obstructing, or impeding the due administration of justice (§ 1503); corruptly altering, destroying, or concealing records to impair their use in an official proceeding (§ 1512(c)); knowingly altering, falsifying, or making a false entry in a record with intent to impede a federal investigation or matter (§ 1519).
Mental state required: corruptly or with intent to obstruct

Full name: Obstructing officers, firefighters, and government functions
Citation: Cal. Penal Code §§ 148(a)(1), 148.2; N.Y. Penal Law § 195.05
What it covers: Willfully resisting, delaying, or obstructing a public officer, peace officer, or EMT in the discharge of duty (Cal. § 148(a)(1)); willfully resisting or interfering with firefighters or emergency rescue personnel at a fire or emergency (§ 148.2); intentionally obstructing governmental administration or preventing a public servant from performing an official function by intimidation, physical force, interference, or an independently unlawful act (N.Y. § 195.05).

Full name: Offering or preparing false evidence (California)
What it covers: Offering in evidence, as genuine, any writing or record knowing it forged or fraudulently altered (§ 132); preparing any false or antedated record or other matter with intent to produce it as genuine in a legal proceeding for a fraudulent or deceitful purpose (§ 134). Both felonies.

Full name: Espionage and economic espionage
What it covers: Gathering, transmitting, or losing national defense information with intent or reason to believe it will injure the United States or advantage a foreign nation (§§ 793, 794); stealing or misappropriating trade secrets intending or knowing the offense will benefit a foreign government, instrumentality, or agent (§ 1831).
Mental state required: intent or reason to believe; knowledge

Full name: Forced labor and trafficking
What it covers: Knowingly obtaining labor or services by force, physical restraint, serious harm, abuse of law or legal process, or a scheme to make a person believe they will suffer serious harm (forced labor); recruiting, harboring, or transporting a person for such labor; sex trafficking of children or by force, fraud, or coercion.

Full name: Trafficking Victims Protection Reauthorization Act civil remedy
What it covers: A trafficking victim may sue the perpetrator or whoever knowingly benefits, financially or by receiving anything of value, from participation in a venture that it knew or should have known engaged in a trafficking violation.

Full name: Transportation and distribution of obscene matter
What it covers: Knowingly using an express company, common carrier, or interactive computer service to carry obscene books, pictures, writings, or other matter in interstate or foreign commerce (§ 1462), or transporting obscene matter, including text and images, for sale or distribution (§ 1465). Reaches adult material only if legally obscene.

Full name: Provider duty to report child sexual abuse material
What it covers: Electronic communication service and remote computing service providers must report to NCMEC's CyberTipline as soon as reasonably possible after obtaining actual knowledge of apparent child sexual exploitation violations listed in the statute; knowing and willful failure to report draws fines (up to $850,000 for an initial failure by providers with 100 million or more monthly active users); providers have limited immunity for reporting conduct, lost for intentional misconduct, actual malice, or reckless disregard (§ 2258B).
Mental state required: knowing and willful failure for fines

Full name: Solicitation of murder and other crimes (California)
What it covers: With intent that the crime be committed, soliciting another to commit or join in the commission of murder (three, six, or nine years); other subdivisions cover solicitation of other listed crimes.
Mental state required: intent that the crime be committed

Full name: Incitement to riot; constitutional incitement limit
Citation: Cal. Penal Code § 404.6(a); Brandenburg v. Ohio, 395 U.S. 444, 447-48 (1969)
What it covers: With intent to cause a riot, urging a riot or acts of force or violence or the burning or destroying of property, under circumstances producing a clear, present, and immediate danger of such acts. Constitutionally, advocacy of force or law violation may be punished only when directed to inciting or producing imminent lawless action and likely to produce it (Brandenburg).

Full name: Explosive threats, false bomb information, and arson affecting commerce
What it covers: Using the mail, telephone, or other instrument of interstate or foreign commerce to willfully make a threat, or maliciously convey false information known to be false, about an attempt to kill, injure, or intimidate any individual or to damage property by fire or an explosive (§ 844(e)); maliciously damaging or destroying by fire or explosive property used in or affecting interstate commerce (§ 844(i)).

Full name: Federal student aid fraud
What it covers: Knowingly and willfully embezzling, misapplying, stealing, or obtaining by fraud, false statement, or forgery any funds, assets, or property provided or insured under the federal student aid programs.

Full name: Electronic distribution of personal information to incite harassment (California)
What it covers: With intent to place another in reasonable fear for safety, electronically distributing, without consent, personal identifying information (including a digital image) or harassing messages about the person, for the purpose of imminently causing unwanted physical contact, injury, or harassment by a third party, where likely to incite it. Misdemeanor.

Full name: Publishing restricted personal information of covered officials
What it covers: Knowingly making restricted personal information about a covered person (federal officers, jurors, witnesses, and others listed) or an immediate family member publicly available, with intent to threaten, intimidate, or incite a crime of violence against them, or knowing it will be used to do so.

Full name: Theft and fraud against elders or dependent adults (California)
What it covers: A person who is not a caretaker and who violates laws against theft, embezzlement, forgery, fraud, or identity theft with respect to an elder's or dependent adult's property or identifying information, knowing or having reason to know the victim's status, faces enhanced punishment (felony-eligible above $950).
Mental state required: knows or reasonably should know of victim's status

Full name: Official misconduct (New York and Wisconsin)
What it covers: A public servant who, to obtain a benefit or deprive another of one, knowingly performs an unauthorized act relating to office or knowingly refrains from a duty (N.Y., class A misdemeanor); a public officer or employee who knowingly exceeds lawful authority or exercises discretionary power inconsistently with duties or others' rights with intent to obtain a dishonest advantage (Wis., Class I felony).

Full name: Unlawful electronic tracking (California and Wisconsin)
What it covers: Using an electronic tracking device to determine a person's location or movement (Cal., subject to statutory exceptions); placing a GPS device on a vehicle owned or leased by another without consent (Wis., Class A misdemeanor; does not apply to law enforcement officers acting in an official capacity, employers tracking their own vehicles, lienholders, or parents of minors).

Full name: California automated license plate reader law
