What it covers: ALPR operators must maintain reasonable security and a public usage and privacy policy; an individual harmed by a violation, including unauthorized access to or use of ALPR information, may sue the person who knowingly caused the harm for actual damages (at least $2,500 liquidated), punitive damages for willful or reckless disregard, fees, and equitable relief.

Full name: Georgia captured license plate data misuse
What it covers: Law enforcement agencies may access captured license plate data only for a law enforcement purpose and must destroy it within 30 months unless needed for one; knowingly requesting, using, or obtaining such data under false pretenses or for any other purpose is a misdemeanor of a high and aggravated nature, and contractors holding the data are bound.

Full name: California Confidentiality of Medical Information Act
What it covers: Health care providers, plans, and contractors may not disclose medical information without authorization except as permitted; individuals may recover $1,000 nominal damages for negligent release without proof of actual damages, plus actual damages.

Full name: Battery and assault (torts)
What it covers: Battery: acting with intent to cause a harmful or offensive contact, or an imminent apprehension of one, where such a contact results; assault: acting with that intent where the other is put in imminent apprehension of such a contact.

Full name: Malicious prosecution and abuse of process
What it covers: Malicious prosecution: initiating or procuring criminal proceedings against a person who is not guilty, without probable cause and primarily for an improper purpose, where the proceedings end in that person's favor (§ 653); abuse of process: using legal process against another primarily to accomplish a purpose for which it is not designed (§ 682).

Full name: Intentional interference with contract
What it covers: Intentionally and improperly interfering with the performance of a contract between another and a third person by inducing or otherwise causing the third person not to perform, causing pecuniary loss.

Full name: Public and private nuisance
Citation: Cal. Civ. Code §§ 3479, 3493; Restatement (Second) of Torts § 821B
What it covers: Anything injurious to health, indecent or offensive to the senses, or obstructing the free use of property so as to interfere with the comfortable enjoyment of life or property, or unlawfully obstructing free passage of a public street or highway, is a nuisance; a private person may sue for a public nuisance only if specially injured; a public nuisance is an unreasonable interference with a right common to the general public.

Full name: DMCA misrepresentation and anticircumvention
What it covers: Knowingly materially misrepresenting in a takedown notice that material is infringing, or that it was removed by mistake, creates liability for resulting damages (§ 512(f)); circumventing a technological measure that effectively controls access to a copyrighted work is prohibited, with civil remedies (§ 1203).

Full name: Anticybersquatting (Lanham Act § 43(d))
What it covers: Registering, trafficking in, or using a domain name identical or confusingly similar to a distinctive mark, or dilutive of a famous mark, with a bad faith intent to profit from that mark.

Full name: CAN-SPAM Act
What it covers: Initiating commercial email with materially false or misleading header information, with deceptive subject headings, or without a functioning return address or opt-out mechanism is unlawful; enforced by the FTC as an unfair or deceptive act and by other agencies, states, and providers.

Full name: Broadcast obscenity and indecency
What it covers: Uttering obscene, indecent, or profane language by means of radio communication is a crime; broadcast licensees may not air obscene material at any time or indecent material between 6 a.m. and 10 p.m. Applies to over-the-air radio and television broadcasting.

Full name: Monopolization and tying (Sherman § 2, Clayton § 3)
What it covers: Monopolizing, attempting to monopolize, or conspiring to monopolize interstate trade (Sherman § 2, also a felony); leasing or selling goods on the condition that the buyer not use or deal in competitors' goods where the effect may be to substantially lessen competition or tend to create a monopoly (Clayton § 3).
Mental state required: specific intent for attempt; none for monopolization conduct

Full name: California Cartwright Act private action
What it covers: Any person injured in business or property by anything forbidden by California's antitrust chapter may sue for three times the damages, interest, injunctive relief, and fees, whether the person dealt directly or indirectly with the defendant.

Full name: California common pricing algorithm law (A.B. 325)
What it covers: Unlawful to use or distribute a common pricing algorithm (any methodology, including software, used by two or more persons that uses competitor data to recommend, align, stabilize, set, or otherwise influence a price or commercial term) as part of a contract, combination, or conspiracy in restraint of trade, or while coercing another to adopt its recommended price or term; 'distribute' includes licensing or providing access by subscription.
Mental state required: none stated beyond the restraint or coercion

Full name: Commodity Exchange Act manipulation and private action
What it covers: Using any manipulative or deceptive device in connection with swaps or commodity contracts in violation of CFTC rules is unlawful (§ 9(1)); persons who violate the Act are liable for actual damages to those who traded in the affected transactions (§ 25(a)).

Full name: Clean Air Act permits and citizen suits
What it covers: Operating a source that requires a Title V operating permit without one, or violating a permit's requirements, is unlawful (§ 7661a(a)); any person may bring a civil action against a person alleged to be in violation of an emission standard, limitation, or order, or who operates without a required permit (§ 7604(a)).

Full name: Clean Air Act knowing violations
What it covers: Knowingly violating Clean Air Act requirements, including permit and permit-program requirements, is a crime.

Full name: Migratory Bird Treaty Act
Citation: 16 U.S.C. §§ 703(a), 707; United States v. CITGO Petroleum Corp., 801 F.3d 477 (5th Cir. 2015)
What it covers: Pursuing, hunting, taking, capturing, or killing migratory birds by any means without authorization is a misdemeanor; the Fifth Circuit limits 'take' to deliberate acts directed at birds, excluding incidental deaths from otherwise lawful activity, while the Second and Tenth Circuits have read the statute more broadly.

Full name: Rules of the road (California)
What it covers: Stopping for a steady red signal; not driving over a fire hose unless protective jumpers are installed; yielding and stopping for an approaching emergency vehicle sounding a siren and showing a red light; stopping for a school bus displaying flashing red lights and a stop arm.

Full name: Traffic crimes (DUI, fleeing police, passing a stopped school bus)
What it covers: Driving under the influence of alcohol; willfully fleeing or attempting to elude a pursuing marked police vehicle with intent to evade (misdemeanor); passing a stopped school bus displaying its stop signal or flashing red lights (North Carolina Class 1 misdemeanor, $500 minimum fine).
Mental state required: intent to evade for fleeing; none stated for DUI

Full name: California autonomous vehicle testing and deployment rules
Citation: Cal. Veh. Code § 38750; Cal. Code Regs. tit. 13, § 228.00 et seq.
What it covers: Autonomous vehicle testing on public roads requires a properly licensed safety driver able to take immediate manual control and $5 million in insurance, bond, or self-insurance; operation beyond testing requires a DMV-approved application, with additional requirements available for driverless operation.

Full name: AI disclosure in political advertising (Wisconsin and Michigan)
What it covers: Paid political advertisements relating to a Michigan candidate, election, or ballot question (Mich. § 169.259(6)), and audio or video communications paid for by a candidate, party, or political committee with express or issue advocacy (Wis. § 11.1303(2m)), that contain AI-generated synthetic media must carry an AI disclosure: Wisconsin requires 'Contains content generated by AI' at the start and end of audio and an on-screen label throughout video synthetic media (forfeiture up to $1,000 per violation; no liability for broadcasters or hosts unless a responsible committee); Michigan requires a clear and conspicuous statement that the advertisement was generated in whole or substantially by AI. Organic posts that no committee paid for are outside both laws.

Full name: Judicial competence duty
Citation: ABA Model Code of Judicial Conduct Rule 2.5(A) (as adopted by states)
What it covers: A judge shall perform judicial and administrative duties competently and diligently; competence requires the legal knowledge, skill, thoroughness, and preparation reasonably necessary to the judge's responsibilities.

Full name: FTC Safeguards Rule (GLBA)
What it covers: Non-bank financial institutions under FTC jurisdiction must maintain an information security program with a qualified individual, a written risk assessment, and safeguards, and must notify the FTC within 30 days of discovering a security event affecting the information of at least 500 consumers (§ 314.4(j)).

Full name: GLBA pretexting
What it covers: Obtaining or attempting to obtain customer information of a financial institution by false, fictitious, or fraudulent statements to the institution's officers, employees, or agents or to its customers, or by providing forged, counterfeit, lost, or stolen documents; knowing and intentional violations punishable by up to five years.

Full name: Driver's Privacy Protection Act
What it covers: State motor vehicle departments may not knowingly disclose personal information from motor vehicle records except as permitted, and no person may knowingly obtain or disclose such information for an impermissible use; a person who knowingly obtains, discloses, or uses it for an impermissible purpose is liable for actual damages of at least $2,500 liquidated damages.

Full name: Texas and Washington biometric identifier laws
Citation: Tex. Bus. & Com. Code § 503.001; Wash. Rev. Code § 19.375.020
What it covers: Capturing a biometric identifier for a commercial purpose without informing the individual and obtaining consent is prohibited (Texas; civil penalty up to $25,000 per violation in attorney general actions; as amended effective Jan. 1, 2026, excludes AI training on biometric data unless the system is used to uniquely identify a specific individual); enrolling a biometric identifier in a database for a commercial purpose requires notice and consent or a mechanism to prevent later commercial use (Washington).

Full name: Washington My Health My Data Act
What it covers: Regulated entities may not collect consumer health data except with consent for a specified purpose or as necessary to provide a requested product or service, and may not share it without separate consent; violations are unfair or deceptive acts under the Washington Consumer Protection Act (ch. 19.86 RCW).

Full name: Federal Common Rule (human subjects research)
What it covers: Human subjects research conducted or supported by a federal department or agency that has adopted the policy must have IRB approval (risks minimized and reasonable, equitable subject selection, safeguards for subjects vulnerable to coercion or undue influence) and legally effective informed consent obtained in conditions that minimize coercion or undue influence.

Full name: PHS research misconduct rule
What it covers: In Public Health Service-funded research, research misconduct means fabrication, falsification, or plagiarism in proposing, performing, or reviewing research or reporting results, excluding honest error and differences of opinion (§ 93.234); a finding requires a significant departure from accepted practices, intentional, knowing, or reckless commission, and proof by a preponderance of the evidence (§ 93.103). The definition formerly sat at § 93.103.

Full name: New York City biometric identifier information law
What it covers: Commercial establishments (food and drink, entertainment venues, retail) that collect, retain, convert, store, or share customers' biometric identifier information must post a clear and conspicuous notice at customer entrances, and may not sell, lease, trade, or otherwise profit from it; private right of action with notice and cure for the signage requirement and statutory damages ($500 per signage violation). Does not apply to government agencies.
Mental state required: none for signage; negligence or intent tiers for sale

Full name: New York City POST Act (police surveillance technology)
What it covers: The NYPD must publish a surveillance technology impact and use policy for its surveillance technologies (capabilities, rules, safeguards, audit mechanisms, and potentially disparate impacts on protected groups), propose policies for new technology at least 90 days before use, accept 45 days of public comment, and publish addenda for enhancements; the Department of Investigation audits compliance.

Full name: San Francisco ban on city use of face recognition
What it covers: City departments may not obtain, retain, access, or use face recognition technology on city-issued software or devices, or information obtained from it, subject to narrow exceptions (inadvertent receipt that is not requested and is logged in the annual surveillance report; non-removable manufacturer-installed functions that are not used).

Full name: Maryland limits on police facial recognition
What it covers: Law enforcement may use facial recognition technology in criminal investigations only for listed serious crimes (crimes of violence, human trafficking, child abuse, child pornography, hate crimes, listed weapon crimes, and others); may not use it for live or real-time identification, on sketches, or to identify people engaged in protected activity without reasonable suspicion; may compare images only against MVA and mugshot databases unless conditions are met; and may not tell a lineup witness that a suspect was identified by facial recognition.

Full name: DOT unfair and deceptive practices authority; airline preemption
What it covers: The Department of Transportation may investigate and stop unfair or deceptive practices or unfair methods of competition by air carriers and ticket agents; states may not enact or enforce laws related to a price, route, or service of an air carrier.

Full name: Federal Election Campaign Act: foreign nationals and fraudulent misrepresentation
What it covers: Foreign nationals may not directly or indirectly make contributions, donations, expenditures, or independent expenditures in connection with US elections (§ 30121); candidates and their agents may not fraudulently misrepresent themselves as speaking for another candidate or party on a matter damaging to that candidate or party, and no person may fraudulently solicit contributions by such misrepresentation (§ 30124).

Full name: Perjury (California and Texas)
Citation: Cal. Penal Code § 118(a); Tex. Penal Code § 37.02
What it covers: Willfully stating as true, under oath or penalty of perjury, a material matter known to be false (Cal.); making a false statement under oath, or a false unsworn declaration, with intent to deceive and knowledge of its meaning (Tex., Class A misdemeanor).
